name: Accuracy
description: Computes classification accuracy as the number of correct predictions (true positives plus true negatives) divided by the total number of cases. It gives the overall fraction of correct classifications.
notes: The result ranges from 0 to 1. Accuracy can be misleading with imbalanced classes, where always predicting the majority class yields a high but uninformative value.

name: F1 Score
description: Computes the F1 score, the harmonic mean of precision and recall, as 2·TP divided by (2·TP + FP + FN). It balances precision and recall into a single measure of a classifier's performance.
notes: The result ranges from 0 to 1; being a harmonic mean, it is high only when both precision and recall are high. It ignores true negatives, so it suits imbalanced positive-focused tasks.

name: Softmax (Two-Class)
description: Converts two logits a and b into the probability of class A, computed as exp(a)/(exp(a)+exp(b)). This is the two-class softmax, which normalizes the exponentiated scores into a probability that sums to one across the classes.
notes: Only the difference a-b matters, so the result equals the sigmoid 1/(1+exp(-(a-b))). The probability of class B is one minus this value.

name: Logistic Sigmoid Activation
description: Applies the logistic sigmoid activation 1/(1+exp(-x)) to a pre-activation input x, squashing any real value into the open interval (0, 1). It is widely used to turn a neuron output into a probability-like value.
notes: Output is 0.5 at x=0 and saturates toward 0 or 1 for large-magnitude inputs, where gradients vanish. The input x is the raw pre-activation (logit), not itself a probability.

name: Tanh Activation
description: Applies the hyperbolic tangent activation to a pre-activation input x, mapping real values into the range (-1, 1). It is a zero-centered S-shaped nonlinearity commonly used in neural networks.
notes: Being centered at 0 can speed training compared with the logistic sigmoid, but it still saturates and loses gradient for large-magnitude inputs. The input x is the raw pre-activation.

name: Leaky ReLU Activation
description: Applies the leaky ReLU activation as max(a*x, x), passing positive inputs unchanged while letting negative inputs through with a small slope a. This keeps a nonzero gradient for negatives, avoiding the dying-ReLU problem.
notes: a is a small positive leak slope (typically around 0.01); the max form assumes a is between 0 and 1 so positives keep slope 1. With a=0 it reduces to standard ReLU.

name: Softmax (Three-Class)
description: Computes the softmax probability of the first class among three logits z1, z2, z3 as exp(z1) divided by the sum of the exponentials. It turns raw scores into a normalized probability for class 1 in a three-way classification.
notes: This returns only the first class probability; the three class outputs together sum to 1. Softmax depends only on differences between logits, so adding a constant to all leaves it unchanged.

name: Temperature-Scaled Softmax (Two-Class)
description: Computes the temperature-scaled softmax probability of class 1 for two logits z1 and z2, dividing each logit by temperature T before the exponential. Temperature controls how sharp or soft the resulting probability distribution is.
notes: T must be positive; higher T flattens the distribution toward 0.5 while T below 1 sharpens it toward 0 or 1. At T=1 it is the ordinary two-class softmax.

name: Mean Squared Error (Two Samples)
description: Computes the mean squared error over two samples as the average of the squared differences between targets and predictions. It measures average squared prediction error, penalizing large deviations more heavily than small ones.
notes: Because errors are squared, the result is in squared units of the target and is dominated by outliers. Take the square root to obtain the RMSE in the original units.

name: Root Mean Squared Error (Two Samples)
description: Computes the root mean squared error over two samples as the square root of the average squared difference between targets and predictions. It reports the typical prediction error in the same units as the target values.
notes: RMSE is the square root of the MSE and remains sensitive to large outliers because of the squaring inside. It is always at least as large as the mean absolute error.

name: Mean Absolute Error (Two Samples)
description: Computes the mean absolute error over two samples as the average of the absolute differences between targets and predictions. It reports the typical prediction error magnitude in the target's own units.
notes: MAE weights all errors linearly, making it more robust to outliers than squared-error metrics. The result is always non-negative and in the same units as the targets.

name: Binary Cross-Entropy Loss
description: Computes the binary cross-entropy loss for a single example as -(y*ln(p) + (1-y)*ln(1-p)), where y is the true label (0 or 1) and p the predicted probability. It penalizes confident wrong predictions heavily and rewards confident correct ones.
notes: The result is in nats because a natural log is used. p must be strictly between 0 and 1 to avoid an infinite loss; the loss is 0 only when p exactly matches the label.

name: Negative Log-Likelihood (Single Sample)
description: Computes the negative log-likelihood of a single observation as minus the natural log of the predicted probability p assigned to the true outcome. Lower values indicate the model assigned higher probability to what actually happened.
notes: The result is in nats due to the natural log; it is 0 when p=1 and grows without bound as p approaches 0. p is the probability the model gave to the correct class.

name: Euclidean Distance (2D Feature Space)
description: Computes the straight-line Euclidean distance between two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) in a 2D feature space using the hypotenuse of their coordinate differences. It is the most common distance metric for comparing feature vectors.
notes: Using hypot avoids overflow or underflow from squaring large or small coordinate differences. This is the L2 distance; for grid-like paths use the Manhattan (L1) distance instead.

name: Manhattan Distance (2D)
description: Computes the Manhattan (city-block) distance between two 2D points as the sum of the absolute differences of their coordinates. It measures distance along axis-aligned paths rather than in a straight line.
notes: This L1 distance is always at least the Euclidean distance and equals it only when the two points share a coordinate. It is less sensitive to large deviations in a single dimension.

name: Cosine Similarity (2D Vectors)
description: Computes the cosine similarity between two 2D vectors a and b as their dot product divided by the product of their magnitudes. It equals the cosine of the angle between them, measuring orientation similarity independent of length.
notes: The result ranges from -1 (opposite) through 0 (orthogonal) to 1 (same direction). Both vectors must be nonzero, and the measure ignores magnitude, so only direction matters.

name: Exponential Learning Rate Decay
description: Computes an exponentially decayed learning rate as the initial rate lr0 times exp(-k*t), where k is the decay constant and t the epoch or step. It smoothly reduces the step size over training to help convergence.
notes: Larger k decays the rate faster; at t=0 the rate equals lr0 and it approaches 0 as training proceeds but never reaches it. t and k must be defined consistently (per epoch or per step).

name: Cosine Annealing Learning Rate
description: Computes the learning rate at step t under a cosine annealing schedule, smoothly decaying from the maximum rate lmax at t=0 down to the minimum lmin at t=T following a half cosine curve. It gives large updates early and gentle refinement late in training.
notes: Valid for 0 to T; t beyond T makes the cosine repeat and rise again. Rates are unitless multipliers, not percentages, and the decay is nonlinear, being steepest near the middle of the cycle.

name: Sigmoid Derivative
description: Returns the derivative of the sigmoid function expressed directly in terms of its own output s, namely s times (1 minus s). This value is used during backpropagation to scale gradients flowing through a sigmoid activation.
notes: Input s must be the sigmoid output between 0 and 1, not the pre-activation. The result peaks at 0.25 when s=0.5 and vanishes near 0 or 1, which is the source of the vanishing-gradient problem.

name: Softplus Activation
description: Computes the softplus activation ln(1+exp(x)), a smooth, everywhere-differentiable approximation of the ReLU function. The output is always positive and approaches x for large positive inputs and 0 for large negative inputs.
notes: Its derivative is the sigmoid function. For large x a naive exp(x) can overflow, so stable implementations use max(x,0)+ln(1+exp(-|x|)); output is unbounded above.

name: Swish (SiLU) Activation
description: Computes the Swish (also called SiLU) activation, x times the sigmoid of x. It behaves like a smooth ReLU but allows a small negative dip for slightly negative inputs, which often improves deep network training.
notes: Non-monotonic: the output reaches a small minimum below zero before rising. For large positive x it approaches x and for large negative x it approaches 0; input is the raw pre-activation.

name: GELU (Sigmoid Approximation)
description: Computes the sigmoid-based approximation of the GELU activation, x divided by (1+exp(-1.702x)). This closely matches the exact Gaussian-error-linear-unit while being cheaper to evaluate, widely used in transformer models.
notes: This is an approximation; the exact GELU uses the Gaussian CDF and differs slightly. The constant 1.702 is fixed by fitting, and input x is the raw pre-activation.

name: Hinge Loss (SVM)
description: Computes the hinge loss for a single sample, max(0, 1 minus y times s), used to train support vector machines. It is zero when the decision score s has the correct sign and a margin of at least 1, and grows linearly otherwise.
notes: The true label y must be encoded as +1 or -1, not 0/1. Correct predictions inside the margin still incur loss; the loss is not differentiable at the hinge point where y*s equals 1.

name: KL Divergence (Two Outcomes)
description: Computes the Kullback-Leibler divergence from distribution Q to distribution P over two outcomes, measuring in nats how much information is lost when Q approximates the true distribution P. Larger values mean the distributions differ more.
notes: Not symmetric: KL(P||Q) differs from KL(Q||P). Each pair must sum to 1 (p1+p2=1, q1+q2=1) and all q values must be strictly positive, or the log terms break down.

name: Binary Entropy Function
description: Computes the binary entropy of a Bernoulli variable with success probability p, in bits, measuring the average uncertainty of a single yes/no outcome. It is maximal at 1 bit when p=0.5 and zero when p is 0 or 1.
notes: Probability p must lie strictly between 0 and 1; the limits give 0 by convention since 0*log2(0) is taken as 0. Uses log base 2, so the result is in bits rather than nats.

name: Logit (Log-Odds)
description: Computes the logit, or natural log of the odds, of a probability p, mapping a value in (0,1) to the whole real line. It is the inverse of the sigmoid function and linearizes probabilities for logistic regression.
notes: Probability p must be strictly between 0 and 1; p=0.5 gives 0, and values approaching 0 or 1 send the logit to negative or positive infinity respectively.

name: L2 Regularization Penalty
description: Computes the L2 (ridge) regularization penalty for two weights, lambda times the sum of squared weights divided by two. Added to a loss function, it discourages large weights and helps prevent overfitting.
notes: The 1/2 factor is a convention that makes the gradient simply lambda times each weight. The penalty ignores weight sign but grows with magnitude squared, so large weights are penalized disproportionately.

name: Gaussian RBF Kernel
description: Computes the Gaussian radial basis function kernel between two 2D points, exp of minus gamma times their squared Euclidean distance. It gives a similarity value near 1 for close points and near 0 for distant ones.
notes: Gamma controls the kernel width: larger gamma means faster decay and a more local kernel. The output always lies in (0,1], and the exponent uses squared distance, so units of the inputs matter.

name: Standardization (Feature Scaling)
description: Standardizes a feature value by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation, producing a z-score that expresses how many standard deviations the value lies from the mean. It centers data at zero with unit variance.
notes: Mean and standard deviation should come from the training set and be reused for test data. Sigma must be nonzero; the result is unbounded and unitless, with negative values below the mean.

name: Min-Max Normalization
description: Rescales a value to the range 0 to 1 by mapping the minimum lo to 0 and the maximum hi to 1 through a linear transform. It is used to bring features onto a common bounded scale.
notes: Requires hi greater than lo. Values outside the original [lo,hi] range map outside [0,1], and the scaling is sensitive to outliers that stretch the min or max.

name: Number of Mini-Batches
description: Computes how many mini-batches are needed for one epoch by dividing the dataset size n by the batch size b and rounding up. The ceiling accounts for a final partial batch when n is not a multiple of b.
notes: Rounding up means the last batch may contain fewer than b samples. Both inputs should be positive integers; the result is a count of batches per epoch.

name: Gradient Descent Update Step
description: Performs one gradient descent update, subtracting the learning rate times the gradient from the current weight w. This moves the weight in the direction that reduces the loss, by a step proportional to the slope.
notes: Too large a learning rate can overshoot and diverge, while too small a rate learns slowly. The gradient g should be the loss derivative with respect to this weight.

name: Adam Bias-Corrected Moment
description: Applies Adam's bias correction to a moment estimate m by dividing it by (1 minus the decay rate raised to the step t). This compensates for the moment being initialized at zero, which biases early estimates toward zero.
notes: The correction is largest at early steps and fades toward 1 as t grows. Decay rate b must be in (0,1) and t is the 1-based step count; the same formula corrects both first and second moments.

name: Classification Accuracy
description: Computes classification accuracy as the fraction of all predictions that are correct, the sum of true positives and true negatives divided by the total count. It gives an overall success rate between 0 and 1.
notes: Accuracy can be misleading on imbalanced datasets where predicting the majority class scores high. It weights all errors equally, ignoring the difference between false positives and false negatives.

name: Recall (Sensitivity)
description: Computes recall, also called sensitivity or true positive rate, the fraction of actual positives that the model correctly identifies, true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives. High recall means few positives are missed.
notes: Recall ignores false positives, so a model predicting everything positive scores 1. It should be read alongside precision; the denominator counts all real positives, not all predicted positives.

name: Balanced Accuracy
description: Computes balanced accuracy as the average of recall on the positive class and recall on the negative class (specificity). It gives a fairer performance measure than plain accuracy when the two classes are imbalanced.
notes: Each class contributes equally regardless of its size, so majority-class dominance is removed. It equals 0.5 for random or constant predictions and requires nonzero positive and negative totals.

name: F-beta Score
description: Computes the F-beta score, a weighted harmonic mean of precision and recall where beta sets their relative importance. Beta greater than 1 favors recall, while beta less than 1 favors precision; beta=1 gives the balanced F1 score.
notes: Precision and recall are fractions in [0,1]. Beta weights recall beta-squared times as much as precision; the score is 0 if both precision and recall are 0.

name: Matthews Correlation Coefficient
description: Computes the Matthews correlation coefficient, a balanced measure of binary classification quality from the full confusion matrix. It ranges from -1 (total disagreement) through 0 (random) to +1 (perfect prediction).
notes: Reliable even on imbalanced classes because it uses all four counts. If any factor in the denominator is zero the value is undefined and conventionally set to 0.

name: Cohen's Kappa
description: Computes Cohen's kappa, which measures agreement between two raters or a prediction and truth while correcting for the agreement expected by chance. Values near 1 indicate strong agreement beyond chance, and 0 indicates chance-level agreement.
notes: Both inputs are probabilities in [0,1]; observed agreement po should exceed expected pe for a positive result. Kappa can be negative when agreement is worse than chance, and pe must not equal 1.

name: Jaccard Similarity Coefficient
description: Computes the Jaccard similarity coefficient between two sets as the size of their intersection divided by the size of their union. It ranges from 0 for disjoint sets to 1 for identical sets, measuring overlap.
notes: The union is computed as a+b minus the intersection, so the intersection must not exceed either set size. Both sets being empty leaves the value undefined.

name: Adjusted R-Squared
description: Computes adjusted R-squared, which corrects the ordinary R-squared for the number of predictors k so that adding useless variables does not inflate the score. It rewards fit while penalizing model complexity.
notes: Requires n greater than k+1. Unlike R-squared it can decrease and even go negative when extra predictors add no explanatory value; n is the sample size and k the number of predictors.

name: ReLU Activation
description: Applies the ReLU (rectified linear unit) activation, max(0, x), passing positive pre-activations through unchanged while zeroing out negative ones. It is the most widely used activation function in deep neural networks for its simplicity and effectiveness.
notes: ReLU is not differentiable at x=0; implementations conventionally take the derivative there as 0 or 1. Negative inputs produce zero output and zero gradient, which can cause the dying-ReLU problem during training.

name: False Discovery Rate
description: Gives the share of predicted positives that are wrong (1 − precision).
notes: Controlled by the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure in multiple testing.

name: False Omission Rate
description: Gives the share of predicted negatives that are actually positive (1 − negative predictive value).
notes: Matters when a negative result is used to rule a condition out.

name: Markedness
description: Adds precision and negative predictive value and subtracts 1; the predictive counterpart of Youden's J.
notes: MCC is the geometric mean of informedness (Youden's J) and markedness.

name: Fowlkes–Mallows Index
description: Takes the geometric mean of precision and recall; also used to compare two clusterings.
notes: Ignores true negatives, like the F1 score.

name: Critical Success Index (Threat Score, IoU)
description: Gives hits over hits plus misses plus false alarms; also the intersection-over-union of predicted and actual positives.
notes: Standard in weather-forecast verification and image segmentation.

name: Prevalence Threshold
expression: (sqrt((tp / (tp + fn)) * (fp / (fp + tn))) - fp / (fp + tn)) / (tp / (tp + fn) - fp / (fp + tn))
description: Gives the prevalence below which a test's positive predictive value drops sharply (Balayla 2020).
notes: Screening a rarer condition than this produces mostly false positives.

name: Lift of a Classifier
description: Divides precision by the base rate: how many times more likely a flagged case is to be positive than a random one.
notes: Used for marketing response models and fraud rules.

name: Macro-Averaged F1
description: Averages the F1 scores of all classes equally, so rare classes count as much as common ones.
notes: Compare with micro-averaged F1, which is dominated by the largest classes.

name: Micro-Averaged F1
description: Pools the counts of all classes before computing F1. For single-label multiclass tasks it equals accuracy.
notes: Dominated by the frequent classes.

name: Weighted-Average F1
description: Averages per-class F1 scores weighted by how many true examples each class has.
notes: Sits between macro and micro averaging.

name: ROC AUC from Scores (Mann–Whitney)
expression: sum(i, 1, len(sp), sum(j, 1, len(sn), (at(sp, i) > at(sn, j)) + 0.5 * (at(sp, i) == at(sn, j)))) / (len(sp) * len(sn))
description: Gives the area under the ROC curve as the chance that a random positive scores higher than a random negative (ties count half).
notes: 0.5 is random guessing, 1 perfect ranking.

name: Gini Coefficient of a Classifier
expression: 2 * sum(i, 1, len(sp), sum(j, 1, len(sn), (at(sp, i) > at(sn, j)) + 0.5 * (at(sp, i) == at(sn, j)))) / (len(sp) * len(sn)) - 1
description: Gives 2·AUC − 1, the form in which credit-scoring models are usually reported.
notes: Also equals Somers' D between score and outcome.

name: Log Loss (Binary Cross-Entropy over a Dataset)
description: Averages the binary cross-entropy of predicted probabilities over a whole dataset.
notes: Heavily punishes confident wrong answers; lower is better.

name: Brier Score
description: Averages the squared difference between predicted probabilities and outcomes (Brier 1950).
notes: 0 is perfect; always predicting 0.5 scores 0.25.

name: Brier Skill Score
description: Compares the Brier score with that of always predicting the base rate; positive means skill.
notes: Used for weather and sports forecasts.

name: Mean Squared Error of Predictions
description: Averages the squared prediction errors over any number of examples.
notes: Sensitive to outliers because errors are squared.

name: Root Mean Squared Error of Predictions
description: Takes the square root of the mean squared error, in the same units as the target.
notes: Always at least as large as the mean absolute error.

name: Mean Absolute Error of Predictions
description: Averages the absolute prediction errors.
notes: Less sensitive to outliers than RMSE.

name: Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE)
description: Averages the absolute errors as percentages of the true values.
notes: Undefined when a true value is 0 and biased towards under-forecasts.

name: Symmetric MAPE (sMAPE)
description: Scales each absolute error by the average of the true and predicted magnitudes, used in the M3/M4 forecasting competitions.
notes: Ranges from 0 to 200 %.

name: Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE)
description: Divides the forecast MAE by the in-sample MAE of the naive one-step forecast (Hyndman and Koehler 2006).
notes: Below 1 means better than the naive forecast; works even when values are zero.

name: Coefficient of Determination R² of Predictions
description: Gives the share of variance in the target explained by the predictions: 1 − SS_res/SS_tot.
notes: Can be negative when predictions are worse than always predicting the mean.

name: Median Absolute Error
description: Takes the median of the absolute errors, robust to a few very bad predictions.
notes: Half of the errors are smaller than this value.

name: Huber Loss (One Sample)
expression: if(abs(y - p) <= dl, 0.5 * (y - p)^2, dl * (abs(y - p) - 0.5 * dl))
description: Uses squared error for small errors and absolute error for large ones, combining the benefits of MSE and MAE.
notes: The smooth L1 loss used in object detection is the case δ = 1 (divided by δ).

name: Log-Cosh Loss
description: Behaves like half the squared error for small errors and like the absolute error for large ones, and is twice differentiable.
notes: Popular for gradient-boosted regression.

name: Quantile (Pinball) Loss
description: Scores a quantile forecast: under-predictions cost τ per unit and over-predictions 1 − τ.
notes: Minimising it gives quantile regression; used for prediction intervals.

name: Discounted Cumulative Gain (DCG@k)

variables.label: Relevance of results in ranked order

description: Adds the graded relevance of the top k results, discounting lower positions logarithmically (exponential-gain form).
notes: Divide by the ideal DCG for NDCG.

name: Normalised DCG (NDCG@k)
expression: sum(i, 1, min(k, len(rel)), (2^at(rel, i) - 1) / log2(i + 1)) / sum(i, 1, min(k, len(rel)), (2^at(sort(rel), len(rel) + 1 - i) - 1) / log2(i + 1))

variables.label: Relevance of results in ranked order

description: Divides DCG by the DCG of the best possible ordering, giving a score between 0 and 1 for search and recommendation ranking.
notes: The standard metric in learning-to-rank benchmarks.

name: Mean Reciprocal Rank

variables.label: Rank of the first correct answer per query

description: Averages 1/rank of the first relevant result over queries.
notes: Used for question answering and search where only the first hit matters.

name: Average Precision of a Ranked List
expression: sum(k, 1, len(rel), at(rel, k) * sum(j, 1, k, at(rel, j)) / k) / sum(rel)

variables.label: Relevant (1) or not (0), in ranked order

description: Averages the precision at each position where a relevant result appears.
notes: The mean over queries is MAP, a standard retrieval and object-detection metric.

name: Expected Calibration Error
description: Measures how far a model's confidence differs from its accuracy, averaged over confidence bins weighted by bin size.
notes: Modern neural networks are often over-confident; temperature scaling reduces ECE.

name: Wilson Score Interval for Accuracy (Lower)
description: Gives the lower end of the Wilson confidence interval for an accuracy or any proportion measured on n examples.
notes: More reliable than the normal (Wald) interval for small n or accuracies near 0 or 1.

name: Wilson Score Interval for Accuracy (Upper)
description: Gives the upper end of the Wilson confidence interval.
notes: Report both ends when comparing models on small test sets.

name: McNemar Test p-Value (Comparing Two Classifiers)

variables.label: Cases only model A got right
Cases only model B got right

description: Tests whether two classifiers evaluated on the same examples differ in accuracy, using only the cases where they disagree.
notes: A p-value below 0.05 suggests a real difference.

name: Spearman Rank Correlation (No Ties)
expression: 1 - 6 * sum(i, 1, len(x), (sum(j, 1, len(x), at(x, j) < at(x, i)) - sum(j, 1, len(y), at(y, j) < at(y, i)))^2) / (len(x) * (len(x)^2 - 1))
description: Correlates the ranks of two variables: 1 − 6Σd²/(n(n² − 1)), where d is the rank difference. Assumes no tied values.
notes: Captures any monotonic relationship, not just linear ones.

name: Kendall Rank Correlation τ (No Ties)
expression: sum(i, 1, len(x) - 1, sum(j, i + 1, len(x), sign((at(x, i) - at(x, j)) * (at(y, i) - at(y, j))))) * 2 / (len(x) * (len(x) - 1))
description: Counts concordant minus discordant pairs over all pairs (Kendall's τ-a).
notes: Easier to interpret than Spearman: the difference between the probabilities of agreement and disagreement in order.

name: Mean Bias Error
description: Averages the signed errors; positive means the model over-predicts on average.
notes: Errors of opposite sign cancel, so read it together with MAE.

name: Normalised RMSE (by Range)
description: Divides RMSE by the range of the true values so errors can be compared across targets of different scales.
notes: Other versions divide by the mean or the standard deviation instead.

name: Top-k Accuracy from Ranks

variables.label: Rank of the correct class per example

description: Gives the share of examples whose correct class is among the model's top k guesses.
notes: ImageNet results are traditionally reported as top-1 and top-5 accuracy.

name: TF-IDF Weight
description: Weights a term by how often it appears in a document and how rare it is across the collection (Spärck Jones 1972).
notes: Many variants exist (log-scaled tf, smoothed idf).

name: Smoothed IDF (scikit-learn)
description: Gives the smoothed inverse document frequency used by scikit-learn's TfidfVectorizer, which never divides by zero or gives a zero weight.
notes: Adds one to both counts as if an extra document contained every term.

name: BM25 Term Score
description: Scores how well one query term matches a document with Okapi BM25, which saturates term frequency and normalises for document length (Robertson et al. 1994).
notes: Sum over the query terms for the document score; still a strong baseline for search and RAG.

name: BM25 Document Score (Several Terms)
description: Adds the BM25 scores of all query terms for one document.
notes: Rare terms contribute most.

name: Reciprocal Rank Fusion Score

variables.label: Rank of the document in each result list

description: Merges several ranked lists (for example keyword and vector search) by adding 1/(k + rank) over the lists (Cormack et al. 2009).
notes: Robust and needs no score calibration; k = 60 is standard for hybrid search.

name: Maximal Marginal Relevance Score
description: Scores a candidate by relevance minus redundancy with what has already been selected (Carbonell and Goldstein 1998).
notes: Used to diversify search results and RAG context.

name: Precision at k

variables.label: Relevant results in the top k

description: Gives the share of the top k results that are relevant.
notes: Ignores the order within the top k.

name: Recall at k

variables.label: Relevant results in the top k

description: Gives the share of all relevant documents that appear in the top k results.
notes: For RAG, the retriever's recall at k bounds what the model can possibly use.

name: InfoNCE Contrastive Loss
expression: -(at(sm, 1) / tmp - (max(sm / tmp) + ln(sum(exp(sm / tmp - max(sm / tmp))))))
description: Computes −ln[exp(s⁺/τ)/Σ exp(sᵢ/τ)]: the loss that trains embedding models such as CLIP and SimCLR to pick the positive among negatives (van den Oord et al. 2018).
notes: CLIP learns τ; 0.07 was its starting value.

name: Word2vec Negative-Sampling Loss

variables.label: Score u·v of the true context word
Scores u·v of the negative samples

description: Gives the skip-gram negative-sampling loss −ln σ(u·v⁺) − Σ ln σ(−u·v⁻) (Mikolov et al. 2013).
notes: Five to twenty negatives per positive are typical.

name: Negative-Sampling Word Probability (Unigram^0.75)
description: Gives the probability of drawing a word as a negative sample in word2vec: counts raised to the power 0.75, normalised.
notes: The 3/4 power boosts rare words relative to plain frequency.

name: Pointwise Mutual Information
description: Measures how much more often two words co-occur than if they were independent.
notes: Positive PMI (max(0, PMI)) matrices underlie classic word embeddings.

name: Type–Token Ratio
description: Gives vocabulary richness as distinct words over total words.
notes: Falls with text length, so compare texts of similar size.

name: Zipf's Law Frequency

variables.label: Frequency of the most common word

description: Predicts the frequency of the word of rank r as C/r^s; in natural language s is close to 1.
notes: The 10th most common word appears about a tenth as often as the most common one.

name: Heaps' Law Vocabulary Size
description: Estimates the number of distinct words in a text of n tokens as K·n^β, with β typically 0.4–0.6 for English.
notes: Vocabulary keeps growing, which is why subword tokenizers are used.

name: Word Error Rate
description: Scores speech recognition or OCR as edit operations per reference word.
notes: Can exceed 100 % when there are many insertions. Character error rate uses characters instead.

name: BLEU Brevity Penalty
description: Penalises translations shorter than the reference in the BLEU metric (Papineni et al. 2002).
notes: No penalty when the candidate is longer.

name: BLEU Score from n-Gram Precisions
expression: if(c > r, 1, exp(1 - r / c)) * gmean(pn) * 100
description: Combines the modified n-gram precisions by a geometric mean and applies the brevity penalty.
notes: Corpus-level BLEU of 30–40 is good for machine translation; single-sentence BLEU is noisy.

name: ROUGE-N F1
description: Combines ROUGE-N precision (overlap/candidate) and recall (overlap/reference) into F1 for summarisation evaluation (Lin 2004).
notes: ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2 use unigrams and bigrams.

name: Perplexity from Token Probabilities

variables.label: Probabilities the model gave to each actual token

description: Computes perplexity directly from the probabilities assigned to the observed tokens.
notes: Equal to the inverse geometric mean of those probabilities.

name: Text Chunk Count with Overlap
description: Gives how many overlapping chunks a document is split into for retrieval-augmented generation.
notes: Overlap keeps sentences that straddle a boundary retrievable.

name: Vector Index Memory (Flat)
description: Gives the memory for storing embeddings uncompressed: vectors × dimensions × bytes.
notes: 10 million 1024-dimensional float32 vectors take about 41 GB.

name: HNSW Graph Index Memory
description: Estimates the memory of an HNSW approximate-nearest-neighbour index: the vectors plus about 2M four-byte neighbour links per node (Malkov and Yashunin 2018).
notes: Upper layers add only a few per cent.

name: Product Quantisation Compression Ratio
description: Gives how much product quantisation shrinks each vector: d floats become m one-byte codes (Jégou et al. 2011).
notes: 1024-d float32 with 64 sub-quantisers compresses 64-fold, at some cost in recall.

name: Least-Squares Coefficients (Normal Equations)

variables.label: Design matrix X (one row per example, first column 1)

description: Solves (XᵀX)β = Xᵀy for the ordinary least-squares coefficients of a linear model with any number of features.
notes: Here intercept 0.15 and slope 1.94. Use the ridge version when features are nearly collinear.

name: Ridge Regression Coefficients
expression: linsolve(mmul(trans(xm), xm) + lam * eye(len(at(xm, 1))), mmul(trans(xm), yv))

variables.label: Design matrix X (one row per example, first column 1)

description: Solves (XᵀX + λI)β = Xᵀy, which shrinks coefficients and stabilises the fit (Hoerl and Kennard 1970).
notes: Usually the intercept is not penalised; centre the data first for that.

name: Simple Linear Regression Prediction
description: Fits a least-squares line to the data and predicts y at a new x.
notes: Extrapolating far beyond the data is risky.

name: Odds Ratio from a Logistic Coefficient
description: Converts a logistic-regression coefficient into the factor by which the odds change when the feature grows by Δx.
notes: β = 0.4 multiplies the odds by about 1.49 per unit.

name: Naive Bayes Posterior (Two Classes)
description: Combines a prior with per-feature likelihoods assumed independent given the class, the classic spam-filter model.
notes: Works surprisingly well even when features are correlated.

name: Laplace (Additive) Smoothing

variables.label: Count of the word in the class

description: Adds α to every count so unseen words get a small non-zero probability.
notes: α = 1 is add-one (Laplace) smoothing; smaller α (Lidstone) is often better.

name: Euclidean Distance (n Dimensions)
description: Gives the straight-line distance between two points with any number of features.
notes: Scale features first, or large-range features dominate.

name: Manhattan Distance (n Dimensions)
description: Adds the absolute differences of the coordinates (L1 or city-block distance).
notes: Less sensitive to a single large difference than Euclidean distance.

name: Minkowski Distance
description: Generalises Manhattan (p = 1) and Euclidean (p = 2) distance; p → ∞ gives the Chebyshev distance.
notes: k-nearest-neighbour libraries expose p as a hyperparameter.

name: Chebyshev Distance
description: Gives the largest coordinate difference, the number of moves a chess king needs.
notes: Used in warehouse and grid planning where diagonal moves cost the same.

name: Mahalanobis Distance
description: Measures distance from a distribution's mean in units of its spread, allowing for correlated features (Mahalanobis 1936).
notes: Widely used for outlier detection; squared, it follows a χ² distribution for normal data.

name: Silhouette Coefficient of a Point

variables.label: Mean distance to its own cluster a
Mean distance to the nearest other cluster b

description: Scores how well a point fits its cluster: near 1 well placed, near 0 on a border, negative probably mis-assigned (Rousseeuw 1987).
notes: Average over all points to judge the number of clusters k.

name: Gini Impurity
description: Gives the chance of mislabelling a random sample if labelled by the node's class distribution; CART splits to reduce it (Breiman et al. 1984).
notes: 0 for a pure node, (k − 1)/k at most.

name: Information Gain of a Split
expression: -sum(pa / sum(pa) * log2(pa / sum(pa))) - sum(lc) / (sum(lc) + sum(rc)) * -sum(lc / sum(lc) * log2(lc / sum(lc))) - sum(rc) / (sum(lc) + sum(rc)) * -sum(rc / sum(rc) * log2(rc / sum(rc)))

variables.label: Class counts in the left child
Class counts in the right child

description: Gives the drop in entropy from splitting a node into two children, the criterion of ID3 and C4.5 (Quinlan).
notes: Counts must be non-zero here (a zero count contributes 0 to entropy).

name: Bootstrap Out-of-Bag Fraction
description: Gives the share of the data a bootstrap sample of size n leaves out; it tends to 1/e ≈ 36.8 %.
notes: Random forests estimate test error from these out-of-bag examples.

name: AdaBoost Learner Weight

variables.label: Weighted error of the weak learner

description: Gives the vote weight of a weak learner in AdaBoost (Freund and Schapire 1997).
notes: Learners at 50 % error get zero weight.

name: SVM Margin Width
description: Gives the width of the gap between the two classes for a linear support-vector machine with weights w (hard margin).
notes: Maximising the margin is equivalent to minimising ‖w‖.

name: RBF Kernel (n Dimensions)
description: Computes the Gaussian radial basis function kernel exp(−γ‖a − b‖²) for vectors of any length.
notes: scikit-learn's default γ is 1/(features × variance).

name: Polynomial Kernel
description: Computes (γ a·b + c)^d, which lets a linear SVM learn polynomial decision boundaries.
notes: Degree 2 captures all pairwise feature interactions.

name: Laplacian Kernel
description: Computes exp(−γ‖a − b‖₁), a kernel based on the Manhattan distance.
notes: Less smooth than the RBF kernel.

name: PCA Explained Variance Ratio
description: Gives the share of total variance captured by principal component k.
notes: Here the first component explains 52.5 %.

name: PCA Cumulative Explained Variance
expression: sum(i, 1, k, at(sort(ev), len(ev) + 1 - i)) / sum(ev)
description: Gives the share of variance kept by the k largest principal components.
notes: Keep enough components to reach, say, 90–95 %.

name: Robust Scaling
description: Centres a value on the median and scales by the interquartile range, so outliers do not distort the scaling.
notes: scikit-learn's RobustScaler.

name: L2 Normalisation of a Vector
description: Scales a vector to unit length; afterwards dot products equal cosine similarities.
notes: Standard before storing embeddings in a vector index.

name: Volume Fraction of a Ball in a Cube
description: Gives the share of a hypercube filled by the inscribed ball; it collapses towards 0 as dimension grows — the curse of dimensionality.
notes: In 10 dimensions only 0.25 % of the cube lies inside the ball.

name: Hoeffding Generalisation Bound (Finite Hypothesis Class)
description: Bounds how far training accuracy can exceed true accuracy for every hypothesis at once, with probability 1 − δ.
notes: The bound grows only with ln|H|.

name: PAC Sample Complexity (Consistent Learner)
description: Gives the number of examples that guarantee error at most ε with probability 1 − δ for a learner that fits the training data perfectly (Valiant 1984).
notes: About 1682 examples here.

name: Isolation Forest Normalising Constant c(n)
description: Gives the average path length of an unsuccessful binary-search-tree search, used to normalise isolation-forest depths (Liu et al. 2008).
notes: For the default sub-sample of 256 it is about 10.24.

name: Isolation Forest Anomaly Score

variables.label: Average path length of the point

description: Turns a point's average isolation depth into a score: near 1 anomalous, well below 0.5 normal.
notes: Anomalies are isolated in few splits.

name: Matrix Factorisation Rating Prediction
description: Predicts a rating as global mean + user bias + item bias + the dot product of latent factors (Koren et al. 2009, Netflix Prize).
notes: The factors are learned from observed ratings.

name: Simple Exponential Smoothing Forecast
description: Updates the forecast as a weighted average of the latest value and the previous forecast (Brown 1956).
notes: Larger α reacts faster, smaller α smooths more.

name: AR(1) h-Step Forecast
description: Forecasts a first-order autoregressive process: the gap from the mean shrinks by φ each step.
notes: Stationary when |φ| < 1.

name: Demographic Parity Difference
description: Gives the gap in how often a model predicts the positive outcome for two groups; 0 means statistical parity.
notes: Ignores whether the groups differ in the true outcome.

name: Disparate Impact Ratio
description: Divides the selection rate of a group by that of the most-selected group; below 0.8 fails the "four-fifths rule" used in US employment guidelines.
notes: 0.7 here, below the 0.8 threshold.

name: Equal Opportunity Difference
description: Gives the gap in true-positive rates between two groups: qualified people should be found equally often (Hardt et al. 2016).

name: Equalised Odds Gap
description: Takes the larger of the true-positive-rate gap and the false-positive-rate gap; equalised odds requires both to be 0.
notes: Fairlearn reports this as equalized_odds_difference.

name: Predictive Parity Difference
description: Gives the gap in precision (positive predictive value) between two groups: a positive prediction should mean the same for everyone.
notes: Cannot hold together with equal error rates when base rates differ (Chouldechova 2017).

name: Laplace Mechanism Noise Scale
description: Gives the scale b of Laplace noise added to a query so that the result is ε-differentially private (Dwork et al. 2006).
notes: Noise standard deviation is √2·b.

name: Gaussian Mechanism Noise Standard Deviation
description: Gives the Gaussian noise σ that makes a query (ε, δ)-differentially private for ε < 1 (Dwork and Roth 2014).
notes: δ should be much smaller than 1/(number of records).

name: Sequential Composition of Privacy Budgets
description: Gives the total privacy loss of k differentially private queries on the same data: the ε values add up.
notes: Advanced composition gives a tighter bound for many queries.

name: Advanced Composition Privacy Bound
expression: sqrt(2 * nq * ln(1 / dp)) * ep + nq * ep * (exp(ep) - 1)
description: Bounds the total ε of k (ε, δ)-private steps as √(2k ln(1/δ′))·ε + kε(e^ε − 1), growing like √k rather than k (Dwork, Rothblum and Vadhan 2010).
notes: The total δ is kδ + δ′.

name: Randomised Response: Truth Probability
description: Gives how often each person reports their true yes/no answer under ε-local differential privacy (Warner 1965).
notes: ε = ln 3 corresponds to the classic coin-flip scheme (truth 75 %).

name: Randomised Response: Unbiased Estimate
description: Recovers the true share of "yes" from randomised answers.
notes: The estimate is noisier than direct questioning; that is the price of privacy.

name: DP-SGD Noise Multiplier Scale
description: Gives the standard deviation of noise added to the averaged gradient in DP-SGD: σC divided by the batch size (Abadi et al. 2016).
notes: Larger batches dilute the noise per example.

name: k-Anonymity Re-identification Risk
description: Gives the worst-case chance of picking out a person in a k-anonymous table, where every record shares its quasi-identifiers with at least k − 1 others (Sweeney 2002).
notes: k-anonymity alone does not stop attribute disclosure; see l-diversity.

name: Federated Averaging Weight
description: Gives the weight of each client's model in FedAvg, proportional to its local data size (McMahan et al. 2017).
notes: The server model is Σ weight × client model.

name: Federated Averaging of Parameters
description: Combines one parameter from several clients into the global model, weighted by data size (FedAvg).
notes: Applied parameter by parameter.

name: Population Stability Index (PSI)
description: Measures how far a feature's distribution has drifted from training; below 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 moderate, above 0.25 significant — a credit-scoring standard.
notes: Bins must not be empty.

name: Kolmogorov–Smirnov Statistic between Two CDFs

variables.label: CDF of sample A at common points
CDF of sample B at the same points

description: Gives the largest vertical gap between two cumulative distributions, a common drift and score-separation test.
notes: In credit scoring, KS between goods and bads measures model power.

name: Conformal Prediction Quantile Level
description: Gives the quantile of calibration scores to use so that prediction sets cover the truth with probability at least 1 − α, with no distribution assumptions (Vovk; Angelopoulos and Bates 2021).
notes: Needs exchangeable data.

name: Conformal Prediction Interval (Regression)
description: Gives the split-conformal interval ŷ ± q̂, where q̂ is the conformal quantile of absolute calibration residuals.
notes: Width is the same everywhere; normalised scores give adaptive widths.

name: Predictive Entropy (Uncertainty)
description: Measures total uncertainty of a classifier's prediction; high values flag inputs to review or to label next (active learning).
notes: Maximum ln k for k classes.

name: Margin Sampling Score
description: Gives the gap between the two most likely classes; the smallest margins are the most informative to label (active learning).
notes: 0.05 here: the model can barely decide.

name: Least-Confidence Score
description: Scores uncertainty as one minus the top class probability, the simplest active-learning query strategy.
notes: Ignores how probability is spread over the other classes.

name: Mutual Information (BALD) from Ensemble Predictions
description: Splits uncertainty: entropy of the averaged prediction minus the average member entropy gives the disagreement (epistemic) part (Houlsby et al. 2011).
notes: High values mean more data would help; the rest is irreducible noise.

name: Temperature-Scaled Confidence (Binary)
description: Calibrates an overconfident network by dividing the logit by a temperature fitted on validation data (Guo et al. 2017).
notes: T > 1 softens the probabilities without changing any predicted class.

name: Shapley Value (Two Features)
description: Gives feature A's fair share of the prediction change, averaging its marginal contribution over both orders — the idea behind SHAP (Lundberg and Lee 2017).
notes: A gets 6 and B gets 4; together they explain the full change of 10.

name: Shapley Value (Three Features, Feature A)
description: Gives feature A's Shapley value from the model output on every subset of three features, with weights 1/3, 1/6, 1/6, 1/3.
notes: Exact computation needs 2ⁿ evaluations; SHAP approximates it.

name: Permutation Feature Importance
description: Gives how much a model's score drops when one feature's values are shuffled, breaking its link to the target (Breiman 2001).
notes: Correlated features share importance and can each look unimportant.

name: Membership Inference Advantage
description: Measures how much better than guessing an attacker can tell whether a record was in the training set; ε-DP bounds it by e^ε − 1 (Yeom et al. 2018).
notes: 0 means the model leaks nothing about membership.

name: Adversarial Perturbation (FGSM)
description: Moves each input by ε in the direction that increases the loss, the fast gradient sign method (Goodfellow et al. 2015).
notes: Changes invisible to people can flip the prediction.

name: Watermark Detection z-Score (Green-List Tokens)
description: Tests whether text carries a green-list watermark: z > 4 is strong evidence of machine generation (Kirchenbauer et al. 2023).
notes: Unwatermarked text has about γT green tokens.

name: Model Card Error Rate Gap across Subgroups
description: Gives the spread between the best- and worst-served subgroups, a headline number for disaggregated evaluation (Mitchell et al. 2019).
notes: Report the subgroup sizes too; small groups give noisy rates.

name: Graph Convolution Symmetric Normalisation
description: Gives the weight a GCN gives node j's features when updating node i, using degrees with self-loops: 1/√((dᵢ + 1)(dⱼ + 1)) (Kipf and Welling 2017).
notes: Keeps high-degree nodes from dominating.

name: Graph Attention Coefficient
description: Normalises LeakyReLU attention scores over a node's neighbours with softmax, as in graph attention networks (Veličković et al. 2018).
notes: Several heads are averaged or concatenated.

name: PageRank Update for One Page
description: Gives one iteration of PageRank: a random-jump share plus the rank passed on by each linking page (Brin and Page 1998).
notes: Iterate until the ranks stop changing.

name: Adamic–Adar Index
description: Scores a potential link by summing 1/ln(degree) over shared neighbours, so rare shared contacts count more (Adamic and Adar 2003).
notes: Common neighbours with degree 1 cannot occur (they would be leaves).

name: Resource Allocation Index
description: Like Adamic–Adar but with weight 1/degree, penalising hubs more strongly (Zhou et al. 2009).
notes: Often the best simple link predictor.

name: Preferential Attachment Score
description: Scores a potential link by the product of degrees: well-connected nodes attract new links (Barabási and Albert 1999).
notes: Needs no neighbour information beyond degrees.

name: Graph Density
description: Gives the share of possible edges present in an undirected graph.
notes: Social networks are usually very sparse (density far below 1 %).

name: Local Clustering Coefficient
description: Gives the share of a node's neighbour pairs that are themselves connected — how cliquish its circle is (Watts and Strogatz 1998).
notes: 1 means all neighbours know each other.

name: Degree Centrality (Normalised)
description: Gives a node's degree as a share of the maximum possible, n − 1.
notes: The simplest measure of how central a node is.

name: Closeness Centrality

variables.label: Shortest-path distances to all other nodes

description: Gives the reciprocal of the average shortest-path distance to all other nodes; high values reach everyone quickly (Bavelas 1950).
notes: Only defined for connected graphs; use harmonic centrality otherwise.

name: Harmonic Centrality
description: Averages the reciprocal distances to other nodes, so unreachable nodes simply add 0 (Marchiori and Latora 2000).
notes: Works on disconnected graphs.

name: Modularity Contribution of a Community
description: Gives one community's share of Newman–Girvan modularity: the fraction of edges inside minus what a random graph with the same degrees would give (Newman 2006).
notes: Sum over communities; above about 0.3 indicates clear structure.

name: Item-Based Collaborative Filtering Prediction

variables.label: Similarity of the target item to rated items

description: Predicts a user's rating of an item as the similarity-weighted average of their ratings of similar items (Sarwar et al. 2001, Amazon).
notes: Keep only the top-k most similar items.

name: Hit Rate at k

variables.label: Users whose held-out item is in the top k

description: Gives the share of users for whom the held-out item appears in the top-k recommendations, a standard offline recommender metric.
notes: Compare only models evaluated with the same k.

name: Catalogue Coverage of Recommendations
description: Gives the share of the catalogue that appears in anyone's recommendations; low coverage means popular items crowd out the long tail.
notes: Accuracy alone rewards recommending bestsellers.

name: Novelty of a Recommendation

variables.label: Share of users who already interacted with the item

description: Scores how surprising a recommended item is by its self-information; popular items have low novelty.
notes: Average over a list for list-level novelty.

name: Intra-List Diversity
description: Gives one minus the average pairwise similarity of recommended items; higher means a more varied list.
notes: Balance against accuracy, e.g. with maximal marginal relevance.

name: Gaussian Process Posterior Mean (One Observation)
description: Gives the GP prediction at x* after one noisy observation with a unit-variance RBF kernel: the prior mean plus k(x*, x₁)/(1 + σₙ²) times the surprise y₁ − μ.
notes: Far from the data, the prediction falls back to the prior mean.

name: Gaussian Process Posterior Variance (One Observation)
description: Gives the remaining uncertainty at x* after one observation (unit-variance RBF kernel): 1 − k(x*, x₁)²/(1 + σₙ²).
notes: Uncertainty shrinks near data and returns to 1 far away.

name: Expected Improvement (Bayesian Optimisation)
expression: (mu - fb - xi) * normcdf((mu - fb - xi) / sg) + sg * normpdf((mu - fb - xi) / sg)
description: Gives the expected amount by which a candidate beats the best result so far under the surrogate model; the most common acquisition function (Jones et al. 1998).
notes: Balances high predicted mean (exploitation) against high uncertainty (exploration).

name: Probability of Improvement
description: Gives the chance a candidate beats the best result so far under a Gaussian surrogate (Kushner 1964).
notes: Tends to exploit too much unless ξ is raised.

name: GP Upper Confidence Bound Acquisition
description: Scores a candidate by an optimistic estimate μ + √β·σ; GP-UCB has proven regret bounds (Srinivas et al. 2010).
notes: Larger β explores more.

name: Jensen–Shannon Divergence
description: Gives a symmetric, bounded version of KL divergence: the average KL of P and Q from their mixture; 0 to 1 bit.
notes: Its square root is a true metric; the original GAN objective minimises it.

name: Beta–Binomial Posterior Mean
description: Updates a Beta(α, β) belief about a success rate after k successes in n trials and gives the posterior mean.
notes: The prior acts like α + β earlier trials.

name: Dirichlet–Multinomial Posterior Mean
description: Gives the posterior mean probability of category k under a symmetric Dirichlet prior — the Bayesian form of additive smoothing.
notes: Unseen categories keep a small probability.

name: Normal–Normal Posterior Mean
expression: (m0 / v0 + n * xb / vs) / (1 / v0 + n / vs)
description: Combines a normal prior with normal data: the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of prior mean and sample mean.
notes: With many observations the data dominates.

name: Normal–Normal Posterior Variance
description: Gives the posterior variance of a normal mean: precisions (inverse variances) add.
notes: Independent of the observed values.

name: Gaussian Mixture Responsibility (Two Components)
expression: w1 * normpdf((x - m1) / s1) / s1 / (w1 * normpdf((x - m1) / s1) / s1 + (1 - w1) * normpdf((x - m2) / s2) / s2)
description: Gives the E-step probability that a point came from component 1 of a two-component Gaussian mixture (Dempster, Laird and Rubin 1977).
notes: The M-step re-estimates weights, means and variances from these responsibilities.

name: Metropolis–Hastings Acceptance Probability

variables.label: Target density at the current point

description: Gives the chance of accepting a proposed MCMC move so that the chain samples the target distribution (Metropolis 1953, Hastings 1970).
notes: With a symmetric proposal the q terms cancel.

name: Gelman–Rubin R-hat
expression: sqrt(((n - 1) / n * wv + bv / n) / wv)
description: Compares the variance between MCMC chains with that within them; values near 1 suggest convergence (Gelman and Rubin 1992).
notes: Modern practice asks for R̂ < 1.01.

name: Importance Sampling Effective Sample Size
description: Gives how many equally weighted samples a set of importance weights is worth (Kish); low values mean a few samples dominate.
notes: Particle filters resample when it falls below half the particles.

name: Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO)
description: Gives the variational lower bound on the log evidence: reconstruction term minus KL to the prior; VAEs and variational inference maximise it.
notes: The gap to the true log evidence is KL(q ‖ true posterior).

name: Gumbel-Max Sample Score
description: Adds Gumbel noise −ln(−ln u) to a logit; the class with the largest score is an exact sample from the softmax (Gumbel-max trick).
notes: Gumbel-softmax replaces the argmax with a temperature softmax to make it differentiable.

name: Kalman Filter Update (Scalar)
description: Blends a prediction with a measurement using the Kalman gain P/(P + R) (Kalman 1960).
notes: The updated variance is (1 − K)·P.

name: Hidden Markov Model Forward Step

variables.label: Emission probability of the observation in j

description: Updates the forward probability of being in state j after the next observation: Σᵢ αᵢ aᵢⱼ × bⱼ(o) (Rabiner 1989).
notes: Rescale each step to avoid underflow on long sequences.

name: Log-Likelihood of Bernoulli Predictions
description: Gives the total log-likelihood of binary outcomes under predicted probabilities; logistic regression maximises it.
notes: Negative and divided by n it is the log loss.

name: Gaussian Log-Likelihood of Residuals
description: Gives the log-likelihood of a regression model with normal errors; used for AIC/BIC and likelihood-ratio tests.
notes: Maximising it over σ gives σ² = mean of r².

name: Softmax Temperature for a Target Top-Class Probability (Two Classes)
description: Gives the temperature that turns a logit gap into a chosen top-class probability for two classes.
notes: Here T = 2 / ln 3 ≈ 1.82.

name: Log-Odds Update from Evidence (Naive Bayes)

variables.label: Likelihood ratios of each piece of evidence

description: Adds the log likelihood ratios of independent evidence to the prior log-odds, the additive form of Bayes' rule used in naive Bayes and credit scorecards.
notes: Convert back with p = 1/(1 + e^(−log-odds)).

name: Chernoff Bound for Majority Vote Error
description: Bounds the chance that a majority vote of n independent classifiers each right with probability p > ½ is wrong, showing why ensembles work (Hoeffding form).
notes: Real ensemble members are correlated, so gains are smaller.

name: Majority Vote Accuracy (Independent Voters)
description: Gives the exact chance that a majority of n independent voters, each right with probability p, is right (Condorcet's jury theorem).
notes: Five 70 % voters reach about 83.7 %.

name: Variance of an Ensemble Average

variables.label: Std of each member's error σ

description: Gives the variance of the average of m equally correlated models: ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/m — the reason random forests decorrelate their trees (Breiman 2001).
notes: Adding members cannot push variance below ρσ².

name: Cross-Entropy between Two Distributions
description: Gives the average bits needed to code samples from P using a code built for Q: H(P) + KL(P ‖ Q).
notes: Minimising it over Q is the usual classification loss.

name: Wasserstein-1 Distance between Two Equal-Size Samples
description: Gives the earth mover's distance between two one-dimensional samples of equal size: sort both and average the gaps.
notes: Used for drift monitoring and in Wasserstein GANs; it stays meaningful when the distributions do not overlap.

name: Top-k Sampling Renormalised Probability
expression: if(at(p, j) >= at(sort(p), len(p) + 1 - k), at(p, j), 0) / sum(i, 1, k, at(sort(p), len(p) + 1 - i))
description: Gives a token's sampling probability after top-k filtering: the k most likely tokens are kept and renormalised, the rest get 0 (Fan et al. 2018).
notes: Ties at the cut-off are all kept here.
